key_terms.meaning: SI stage I: spark (A) to the first pressure rise above the motoring curve (B); about 1 to 2 ms.
SI stage II: B to peak pressure C; the front burns most of the charge.
SI stage III: after peak pressure; the last charge burns during expansion.
Crank angle (degrees) turned in t ms at N rev/min; 1 ms = 18° at 3000 rev/min.
ṁ<sub>b</sub> = ρ<sub>u</sub> A<sub>f</sub> S<sub>b</sub>: unburnt density × flame front area × burning velocity.
dp/dθ ≈ (γ − 1)(dQ/dθ)/V near TDC; about 1 to 3 bar/°CA in a smooth SI engine.
φ = (F/A) ÷ (F/A)<sub>s</sub> = 1/λ; φ > 1 rich, φ < 1 lean.
% iso-octane in an iso-octane/n-heptane blend that knocks like the fuel; sensitivity = RON − MON.
Standard deviation of IMEP ÷ mean IMEP × 100 %; driveability suffers above about 10 %.
Autoignition of the end gas after the spark, before the flame arrives; pressure ringing at a few kHz.
Surface ignition by a hot spot before the spark.
f ≈ 1.84 c ÷ (π B) for the first mode across the bore.
Density (temperature and pressure), time, and composition factors.
Start of injection to start of combustion: physical plus chemical delay.
Fast burning of the fuel mixed during the delay: the heat-release spike.
Burning at the rate fuel and air mix; most of the heat.
A very steep pressure rise from a large premixed burn after a long delay.
R<sub>s</sub> = N<sub>s</sub> ÷ N; ideal gain into a bowl (bore ÷ bowl)².
Radial inward flow from the squish band as the piston nears TDC.
r = (V<sub>s</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>) ÷ V<sub>c</sub>; the bowl is part of V<sub>c</sub>.
Direct injection into a piston bowl; indirect injection into a pre-chamber or swirl chamber.

takeaways: SI combustion has three stages on the p–θ diagram: ignition lag (A to B), flame propagation (B to peak C) and afterburning.
Ignition lag is roughly fixed in milliseconds, so the spark is advanced as speed rises; flame propagation keeps about the same crank degrees.
The mass burning rate ρ<sub>u</sub> A<sub>f</sub> S<sub>b</sub> sets the heat release, and dp/dθ ≈ (γ − 1)(dQ/dθ)/V near TDC sets the slope of the trace.
Gasoline is judged by volatility, octane number, calorific value and air–fuel ratio; E20 carries almost the same energy per kg of mixture as petrol.
No two cycles burn alike; COV<sub>imep</sub> measures the scatter, and the fastest cycles set the knock limit.
Knock is end-gas autoignition after the spark; pre-ignition is hot-spot ignition before it; retarding the spark cures only knock.
Knock factors come in three groups: density, time and composition.
CI combustion runs through delay, premixed, mixing-controlled and late burning; the delay decides how much fuel burns at once.
Diesel knock comes at the start of combustion from a long delay, so its cures are the opposite of SI knock's.
Swirl, squish and tumble store energy as organised flow and release it as turbulence near TDC; chambers are shaped to use them.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the stages of SI and CI combustion with a labelled p–θ or heat release diagram, the factors affecting knock and the delay period, and the types of combustion chamber; numerical questions convert milliseconds to crank angle and read slopes from a pressure trace. Each long answer below gives the points to cover and a full model answer.

bank.q: Explain the stages of combustion in an SI engine with a neat p–θ diagram. How are the flame front, flame velocity and rate of pressure rise related?
outline: p–θ diagram with motoring curve; points A (spark), B (first rise), C (peak)
Ignition lag: kernel growth, chemical and physical, about 1 to 2 ms
Flame propagation: front, turbulence, bulk of the pressure rise
Afterburning
Three speeds: laminar, turbulent burning, flame travel
ṁ<sub>b</sub> = ρ<sub>u</sub> A<sub>f</sub> S<sub>b</sub> and dp/dθ ≈ (γ − 1)(dQ/dθ)/V

answer.text: Draw the p–θ diagram. Plot cylinder pressure against crank angle, with the motoring curve (engine turned over with no combustion) dashed and the firing curve solid. Mark A at the spark, B where the firing curve leaves the motoring curve and C at peak pressure. The sketch below uses the worked examples' petrol engine at 3000 rev/min: spark at 28° bTDC, B at 10° bTDC, C at 50.3 bar and 15.6° aTDC.

svg.aria: Sketch of the SI p-theta diagram with the three stages marked.

answer: Stage I, ignition lag (A to B). The spark leaves a small kernel of burning gas. It must grow and build up radicals before burning becomes self-sustaining. The lag is both chemical (pre-flame reactions) and physical (kernel growth against heat loss to the electrodes). It lasts about 1 to 2 ms and is shortest with a slightly rich, hot, undiluted mixture and a strong spark. Pressure does not yet differ from motoring.

Stage II, flame propagation (B to C). A thin flame front spreads from the kernel through the charge. Turbulence wrinkles it and raises its area. Because burnt gas is three to four times less dense than unburnt gas, the burning gas expands and compresses the charge ahead, including the end gas. Most of the charge burns here, so the pressure rises steeply and peaks at C, normally 12° to 18° aTDC.

Stage III, afterburning (after C). Charge near the walls, in crevices and behind the front finishes burning while the piston moves down, so the pressure falls. It adds little work; heavy afterburning raises exhaust temperature and hydrocarbons.

Speed and spark advance. The lag is roughly fixed in milliseconds, θ = 0.006 N t, so at 3000 rev/min a 1.0 ms lag is 18° and at 4500 rev/min 27°. Flame propagation speeds up with turbulence and keeps about the same degrees, so the spark is advanced with speed.

Flame speeds. The laminar burning velocity SL is about 0.3 to 0.5 m/s for petrol–air at room conditions. The turbulent burning velocity ST ≈ SL + u′ is a few m/s in an engine. The flame travel velocity across the chamber, relative to the head, is 15 to 40 m/s because the burnt gas pushes the front outward.

Front area and mass burning rate. ṁb = ρu Af Sb. The front area grows from zero at the plug, is largest mid-burn and shrinks as the front meets the walls, giving the S-shaped mass fraction burned curve.

answer.text: Rate of pressure rise. From the first law, dp/dθ = [(γ − 1) dQ/dθ − γ p dV/dθ]/V; near TDC dp/dθ ≈ (γ − 1)(dQ/dθ)/V. For the worked examples' petrol engine (Vc = 62.4 cm³, ρu = 12 kg/m³, front radius 35 mm in a 10.75 mm deep disc, Sb = 6 m/s):

answer: Check and conclusion: 1.49 bar/°CA lies in the 1 to 3 bar/°CA of a smooth engine. A faster burn raises the slope and gives an earlier, higher peak and more work, but rougher running; a slow burn peaks late and wastes heat.

bank.q: Distinguish between knock, detonation and pre-ignition in an SI engine. Explain the autoignition theory of knock and the effects of knock, with p–θ sketches.
outline: End gas and the race with the flame
Knock after the spark, ringing at a few kHz
Detonation as shock-driven severe knock (or the same word)
Surface ignition, pre-ignition and post-ignition, run-on
Effects: noise, damage, heat transfer, power loss, pre-ignition
Sketches: normal, knocking, pre-ignition
answer: End gas. In normal combustion one flame front from the plug burns the charge. The last 5 to 25 % of the charge, the end gas, is compressed by the expanding burnt gas and the piston, so its temperature rises before the flame arrives.

Autoignition theory. A hot fuel–air mixture ignites by itself after an ignition delay τ. If the flame reaches the end gas before τ runs out, combustion is normal. If τ runs out first, the end gas ignites at many points almost at once. The sudden local pressure rise sends pressure waves round the chamber; they reflect and ring at f ≈ 1.84 c/(π B), about 6.5 kHz for an 86 mm bore and c = 950 m/s. This is knock, heard as pinking.

answer.text: Worked check. At 3000 rev/min (18 °/ms) the flame has 20 mm left at TDC and moves at 25 m/s:
answer.pre:
flame arrives after 0.020/25 = 0.8 ms = 14.4°  → 14.4° aTDC
fuel A: τ = 0.6 ms = 10.8° → autoignition 10.8° aTDC → knock
fuel B: τ = 1.0 ms = 18°   → flame arrives first   → no knock

answer: Detonation. Many books use the word for knock itself. Strictly, detonation is a shock-driven combustion wave faster than sound in the unburnt gas; severe knock can approach it, with very high local pressures that erode the piston crown.

Pre-ignition. Surface ignition by a hot spot (overheated plug, glowing deposit, hot exhaust valve) before the spark. It starts the burn while the charge is still being compressed, so peak pressure and heat flux rise sharply near TDC; the hot spot heats further and each cycle pre-ignites earlier. If the hot spot fires after the spark it is post-ignition, a second flame. Run-on (dieseling) is a hot spot firing the engine after the ignition is off.

answer.text: p–θ sketches. Normal: smooth rise to one peak about 15° aTDC. Knock: the same trace with oscillations starting near peak pressure, after the spark. Pre-ignition: the rise starts before the spark, with a much higher peak near TDC.

svg.aria: Sketch of normal, knocking and pre-ignition pressure traces.

answer.text: Differences at a glance.

head: Knock
Pre-ignition
rows: end gas, far from the plug

answer: Effects of knock. Noise and vibration; pitted or holed pistons, broken ring lands, blown gaskets and bearing damage; higher heat transfer because the waves strip the boundary layer, so lower power and efficiency; and overheated surfaces that lead to pre-ignition. Knock and pre-ignition feed each other.
Conclusion: knock is a race lost by the flame; pre-ignition is a race started too early. Classify an event by comparing its angle with the spark angle, not with TDC.

bank.q: Explain the stages of combustion in a CI engine with a heat release rate diagram. Discuss the factors that affect the delay period.
outline: Heterogeneous charge, mixture formation
Delay (physical, chemical), premixed, mixing-controlled, late burning
Heat release diagram marked A to D
Factor table: CR, inlet temperature and pressure, cetane, injection pressure, timing, load, speed
θ<sub>d</sub> = 0.006 N t<sub>d</sub> with a number
answer: Charge. A CI engine compresses air alone to r ≈ 17, giving 800 to 900 K near TDC. Fuel injected near TDC atomises, vaporises and mixes; the charge is heterogeneous and burns only where the local mixture is near stoichiometric, though the overall mixture is lean.

answer.text: Heat release diagram. Plot dQ/dθ against crank angle. The sketch uses the worked examples' diesel at 2000 rev/min: injection of 40 mg from 15° bTDC to 10° aTDC, delay 0.9 ms.

svg.aria: Sketch of a diesel heat release rate diagram with four stages.

answer.text: Stage 1, ignition delay (A to B). From the start of injection to the start of combustion. Physical delay: atomisation, vaporisation, mixing. Chemical delay: pre-flame reactions. For the example:

answer: Stage 2, premixed combustion (B to C). The fuel mixed during the delay ignites at many points and burns in a few degrees: a sharp spike in dQ/dθ and the steepest pressure rise. Its size grows with the delay.

Stage 3, mixing-controlled combustion (C to D). The rest of the fuel burns in diffusion flames as fast as it mixes with air. The rate follows the injection rate and air motion; most of the heat is released here.
Stage 4, late combustion (after D). After injection ends, the last fuel, soot and CO burn slowly in expansion. A long tail means lost work, smoke and hot exhaust.

answer.text: Factors affecting the delay.

head: Factor raised
Delay
Reason
rows: falls in ms, rises in degrees

answer: Injection timing has an optimum about 10° to 15° bTDC, where the air is hottest; earlier or much later injection lengthens the delay. A cold start at cranking speed gives the longest delay and the loudest knock.

Late injection or a low-cetane fuel moves the premixed spike and the whole burn later, so peak pressure falls and exhaust temperature rises, while too early injection lengthens the delay and enlarges the spike: injection timing is a trade between noise and efficiency.
Check: at 2500 rev/min the same engine has a 0.8 ms delay, which is 15 × 0.8 = 12.0°: shorter in time, longer in degrees, so injection is advanced at higher speed.

answer: Swirl is rotation of the charge about the cylinder axis. It is produced during intake by a directed (tangential) port, a helical port that spins the air before the valve, or a shrouded (masked) valve that admits air on one side; the shroud lowers volumetric efficiency, so helical ports are usual.

answer.text: Swirl ratio Rs = Ns/N, the swirl speed over the engine speed, with no unit; DI diesels use about 1 to 3. For the worked examples' petrol engine at 2000 rev/min with Rs = 2.2:
answer.pre:
N<sub>s</sub> = 2.2 × 2000 = 4400 rev/min
ω = 2π × 4400/60 = 460.8 rad/s;  v<sub>wall</sub> = 460.8 × 0.050 = 23.0 m/s
mean piston speed = 2 × 0.110 × 2000/60 = 7.33 m/s
ideal bowl swirl ratio = 2.2 × (100/60)² = 6.1

answer: Swirl speeds up as the air enters the bowl near TDC because its angular momentum is roughly kept while its radius shrinks; friction makes the real gain smaller than (bore/bowl)².

Squish is the radial inward flow when the piston crown nears a flat part of the head (the squish band, about 1 mm gap in a diesel). It is strongest in the last few degrees before TDC and reverses after TDC. It is a squeezing flow, not a rotation.

Tumble is rotation about an axis across the cylinder, produced by steep inlet ports in pent-roof heads. The rising piston flattens the vortex until it breaks into turbulence near TDC; the tumble ratio is defined like the swirl ratio.

Importance in CI engines. Fuel has 1 to 2 ms to find air. Swirl carries air past the sprays and squish drives it into the bowl, so the mixing-controlled stage is shorter, smoke falls and more of the air is used.

Importance in SI engines. Turbulence from tumble and squish raises the burning velocity several times, shortens the burn, lowers cycle-to-cycle variation, resists knock (time factor) and allows leaner mixtures and more EGR.
Measurement: swirl is measured on a steady-flow rig with a paddle wheel or impulse meter behind the head; the swirl ratio quoted for an engine is that measured value scaled to engine speed.
Limits: too much motion raises heat loss to the walls, pumping loss and, in diesels, makes spray plumes overlap. The right amount is a balance, matched to the chamber.

bank.q: An SI engine runs at 3600 rev/min with the spark at 30° bTDC. The ignition lag is 0.9 ms. Its trace reads 22 bar at 2° bTDC and 48 bar at 12° aTDC, and peaks at 16° aTDC. The flame travels 42 mm from the plug to the far wall during flame propagation. Find (a) the lag in degrees and the angle of first pressure rise, (b) the average rate of pressure rise between the two readings in bar/°CA and bar/ms, (c) the duration of flame propagation in degrees and ms and the mean flame travel velocity. (d) Comment on the spark timing.
outline: Signed angles: bTDC negative
Average slope Δp/Δθ and conversion to bar/ms
Stage II from B to the peak; velocity = distance ÷ time
Comment: peak in the 12° to 18° aTDC band
answer: Method. Measure all angles from TDC, with angles before TDC negative, so that adding a duration to a start angle gives the end angle directly. Convert time to crank angle with θ = 0.006 N t (t in ms): the crank turns 360° per revolution and N/60 revolutions per second, so 6N degrees per second, or 0.006N degrees per millisecond.
Degrees per ms: 0.006 × 3600 = 21.6 °/ms.

answer.text: (b) Average rate of pressure rise:

answer: Why the average is useful: the steepest slope of a real trace lies inside the interval and is higher, but two readings from an indicator diagram give only the average. A smooth SI engine stays near 1 to 3 bar/°CA; much more gives rough running and high bearing loads.
(c) Flame propagation runs from B (-10.56°) to the peak (+16°): 16 − (-10.56) = 26.56°. In time: 26.56 ÷ 21.6 = 1.230 ms.
Mean flame travel velocity = 0.042 m ÷ 0.001230 s = 34.2 m/s. This is a flame travel velocity relative to the head; the burning velocity relative to the unburnt gas is only a few m/s.

The difference matters: the front burns into the unburnt gas at S<sub>T</sub> ≈ S<sub>L</sub> + u′, and the expanding burnt gas behind it pushes it outward three to four times faster. Mass burning rate is ρ<sub>u</sub> A<sub>f</sub> S<sub>b</sub>, so it is S<sub>b</sub>, not the travel velocity, that sets the heat release.

(d) The peak at 16° aTDC lies in the usual 12° to 18° band, so the timing is about right. If the lag stayed 0.9 ms at 4500 rev/min (27 °/ms, so 24.3°), the spark would need 34.9° bTDC to keep B at 10.56° bTDC. A peak much later than 18° aTDC would mean too little advance (lost work, hot exhaust); much earlier than 12° would mean too much (high peak pressure, knock risk).

answer.text: Summary of results:

answer: Check: 1.86 bar/°CA is within the 1 to 3 bar/°CA of a smooth engine, and 34 m/s lies in the 15 to 40 m/s range of flame travel velocities.

bank.q: (a) List the properties of gasoline that affect SI engine operation and explain the role of volatility. (b) Find the stoichiometric air–fuel ratio of n-heptane, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>, and the value of λ for an air–fuel ratio of 16.2 on petrol (stoichiometric 14.7). (c) Eight cycles give IMEP 8.62, 8.75, 8.41, 8.80, 8.55, 8.69, 8.38 and 8.72 bar. Find COV<sub>imep</sub> and comment.
outline: Property list with typical values
Distillation curve: 10, 50, 90 % points; Reid vapour pressure; vapour lock
Balanced equation, molar masses
λ and φ
Mean, deviations, s with n − 1, COV and the 10 % guide

answer.text: (a) Properties.

head: Property
Typical value
Effect
rows: starting, warm-up, vapour lock, oil dilution

answer: Octane number is the percentage of iso-octane in an iso-octane–n-heptane blend that knocks like the fuel in a standard engine. RON (600 rev/min, cool intake) is higher than MON (900 rev/min, hot intake); their difference is the sensitivity. Ethanol raises the octane number, which is one gain of E20 petrol.

Volatility. The distillation curve gives the temperatures at which 10 %, 50 % and 90 % of the fuel has boiled off. A low 10 % point eases cold starting but, if too low, causes vapour lock in hot fuel lines. The 50 % point governs warm-up and smooth acceleration. A high 90 % point leaves heavy ends that dilute the oil, form deposits and waste fuel. The Reid vapour pressure at 37.8 °C measures the front end directly.

answer.text: (b) n-heptane.

answer: Real petrol is a blend, so its stoichiometric ratio (about 14.7) lies a little below that of n-heptane or iso-octane (15.1), because aromatics carry less hydrogen per carbon.
λ = 16.2 ÷ 14.7 = 1.102; φ = 1/λ = 0.907. The mixture is lean, with about 10 % excess air: good for economy, but the flame is slower and the lag longer, so cycle-to-cycle variation grows.

answer.text: (c) COVimep.

answer: Comment: 1.8 % is well below the guide of about 10 %, so combustion is stable. A rise towards 10 % would show as roughness and would point to a lean mixture, heavy dilution, weak spark or poor turbulence near the plug; the cures are a faster, more robust early flame: more turbulence near the plug, a stronger spark, less dilution and a mixture closer to λ = 1.

bank.q: A diesel runs at 1500 rev/min. Injection starts at 18° bTDC and delivers 30 mg at a steady rate over 25°. On fuel A the delay is 1.2 ms; on a higher-cetane fuel B it is 0.8 ms. (a) For each fuel find the delay in degrees, the start of combustion and the fuel injected before ignition. (b) Explain why fuel B runs more quietly. (c) Describe four other methods of controlling diesel knock.
outline: θ<sub>d</sub> = 0.006 N t<sub>d</sub>
Start of combustion = start of injection + delay
Fuel waiting = injection rate × delay
Premixed spike and dp/dθ
Methods: CR, intake temperature and boost, timing, pilot injection, atomisation, chamber
answer: Degrees per ms: 0.006 × 1500 = 9.0 °/ms. Injection rate: 30 ÷ 25 = 1.2 mg/°.

answer.text: (a) Results:

answer: (b) Diesel knock is the steep pressure rise of a large premixed burn. With fuel B only 8.64 mg waits at ignition instead of 12.96 mg, a third less, so the premixed spike is smaller and the rate of pressure rise lower. The computed traces in the diesel knock chapter for a similar pair show the steepest rise falling from 8.8 to 6.3 bar/°CA. Fuel B also starts earlier, so its peak pressure may be a little higher: knock is judged by dp/dθ, not by peak pressure.

answer.text: The effect on the pressure trace, from the worked examples' diesel: the shorter delay gives a gentler rise although it starts earlier.

svg.aria: Sketch of two diesel pressure traces with long and short delay.

answer: (c) Other methods. (1) Raise the air temperature and density at injection: a higher compression ratio, boost, an intake heater at cold start, or a glow plug heating the chamber air; all shorten the delay. (2) Keep injection timing near the optimum, about 10° to 15° bTDC, where the air is hottest. (3) Pilot injection or a low initial injection rate: a small first shot ignites and the main shot meets a flame, so less fuel collects. (4) Finer atomisation by higher injection pressure and clean nozzles, shortening the physical delay. (5) Chamber design: good swirl and squish, hot surfaces, or an indirect injection chamber for quiet running.

Cold start: at a cranking speed of 200 rev/min a delay of 4 ms is only 0.006 × 200 × 4 = 4.8°, yet it is a long time for fuel to collect in cold air; that is why the first firing strokes are the loudest.

Check: the delay in degrees, not just in milliseconds, decides how much fuel collects; at a higher speed the same 1.2 ms would be more degrees and more fuel, which is why injection is advanced with speed.

bank.q: A DI diesel has bore 90 mm and stroke 100 mm. Its piston bowl is 50 mm across and 15 mm deep, the squish gap is 0.9 mm over the full bore and valve recesses add 0.6 cm³. (a) Find the clearance volume, the compression ratio and the bowl's share. (b) Compare DI and IDI chambers and say which you would choose for a city car and for a small water-pump engine.
outline: Swept volume, bowl as a cylinder, squish volume
r = (V<sub>s</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>)/V<sub>c</sub>
DI: open bowl, multi-hole, high pressure, economy, noise
IDI: swirl or pre-chamber, pintle, quiet, heat loss, glow plug
Justified choice

answer.text: (a) Volumes:

answer: So about 82 % of the air sits in the bowl at TDC, where the sprays and the amplified swirl meet it; the bowl is part of V<sub>c</sub> and is not added again.

Swirl in the bowl: if the in-cylinder swirl ratio is 2.0, the ideal bowl swirl ratio is 2.0 × (90/50)² = 6.5; friction makes the real gain smaller, but the bowl clearly spins the air faster than the cylinder.

Types within each family. DI: shallow open (quiescent) chambers for large slow engines, where multi-hole sprays do the mixing; deep hemispherical, cylindrical, toroidal and re-entrant bowls for smaller, faster engines, using swirl and squish. IDI: swirl chambers (such as the Ricardo Comet), pre-combustion chambers, and air-cell or energy-cell designs.

answer.text: (b) DI against IDI.

head: Feature
DI (open bowl)
IDI (swirl or pre-chamber)
rows: strong swirl or a burning jet through the throat
10 to 15 % worse: throat and extra surface

answer: City car: DI with common-rail injection, for economy and low CO2; pilot injection keeps it quiet. Small water-pump engine: either works; IDI suits poor fuel, rough service and simple low-pressure pumps, while a simple DI engine gives better fuel economy if the fuel is good. State the reason for the choice, not just the name.

Design points for the DI bowl. The injector sits on the cylinder axis with five to eight holes; the spray angle and length must reach the bowl lip without wetting the cold wall, or the fuel burns late and makes smoke. A re-entrant lip turns the spray back into the bowl and keeps the swirl strong after TDC. The squish gap must be small (about 1 mm) so that almost all the air is in the bowl, but large enough to clear the valves and allow for bearing wear.
Check: r = 18.8 is typical of small DI diesels (about 16 to 19), and the bowl share above 80 % matches a re-entrant or toroidal bowl design.

bank.q: A petrol engine that ran well begins to knock after a tune-up that raised its compression ratio from 8.5 to 10 and advanced the spark from 20° to 28° bTDC at 2500 rev/min. Analyse what happened using the factors affecting knock, with numbers where possible, and recommend corrective steps.
outline: End-of-compression temperature for both ratios
Efficiency gain
Lag and start of burn shift with advance
Group each change: density factors
Correctives from all three groups, with reasons
Judgement: knock limit and knock sensor

answer.text: Compression ratio. With intake at 320 K and n = 1.35, T2 = T1 r0.35:

answer: The charge now ends compression 40 K hotter and at a higher pressure, so the end gas starts much closer to autoignition and its delay τ is shorter. The efficiency gain (2.7 points) is real, but it came with less knock margin. This is a density factor.

answer.text: Spark advance. At 2500 rev/min, 0.006 × 2500 = 15 °/ms. With a lag of 1.1 ms (16.5°):
answer.pre:
spark 20° bTDC → burn starts at −20 + 16.5 = 3.5° bTDC
spark 28° bTDC → burn starts at −28 + 16.5 = 11.5° bTDC

answer: The burn now starts 8° earlier, so most of the heat is released before and just after TDC; peak pressure is higher and earlier, and the end gas is squeezed to a higher temperature while it waits. Another density factor, acting on top of the first.

Why both together are worse than either alone. The end gas starts hotter (compression ratio) and is then compressed harder and longer (advance). The flame travel time is unchanged (same speed, chamber and turbulence), so τ now runs out before the flame arrives.

answer.text: Corrective steps, by group.

head: Step
Group
How it helps
rows: Retard the spark to the knock limit
lower peak pressure and end-gas temperature
longer τ at the same state
Return to a lower ratio (thicker gasket or original pistons)
Cool the intake and check the cooling system and thermostat
removes hot spots and the extra compression they add
Improve squish or move to a central plug (design)
Avoid mixtures near φ = 1.1 at full load

answer: Does the extra efficiency survive? If the spark has to be retarded by several degrees to stop knock, peak pressure moves later and much of the gain from r = 10 is lost. If the engine needs premium fuel at 95 RON instead, the gain is kept, but the running cost rises. The tune-up should be judged on fuel used per km at the knock limit, not on the compression ratio alone.
Avoid the false cures: running the engine slower at full throttle (low speed raises knock), and a weaker spark (lengthens the burn).

Evaluation. The best answer keeps the higher compression ratio for its efficiency and buys back the knock margin by retarding the spark only where needed and using the right fuel. Modern engines do this automatically with a knock sensor that retards the spark of the knocking cylinder for a few cycles. Without a sensor, the tune-up should have raised either the ratio or the advance, not both, and only with a fuel change.

bank.q: Compare knock in SI and CI engines: where and when it occurs, its cause and the methods used to control it. Explain why the factors that reduce knock in one engine increase it in the other.
outline: SI: end gas, end of combustion, autoignition too early
CI: start of combustion, long delay, ignition too late
Comparison table of controls
Reason for the reversal
Numbers from both engines
Judgement
answer: SI knock. Occurs near the end of combustion, in the end gas far from the plug, after the spark. The end gas autoignites before the flame reaches it. For the worked examples' petrol engine at 3000 rev/min, an end gas with a 0.6 ms delay ignites at 10.8° aTDC while the flame is due at 14.4° aTDC: knock. A 1.0 ms delay (higher octane) removes it.

CI knock. Occurs at the start of combustion. Fuel injected during a long delay collects and burns all at once in the premixed stage. For the worked examples' diesel at 2000 rev/min (injection 1.6 mg/° from 15° bTDC), a 0.9 ms delay lets 17.3 mg collect, a 0.5 ms delay only 9.6 mg; the steepest pressure rise falls from 8.8 to 6.3 bar/°CA.

answer.text: Comparison.

head: SI engine
CI engine
rows: injection near the optimum, pilot shot

answer.text: Why the reversal. In both engines knock is the sudden burning of a mass of mixture that has had time to prepare. In the SI engine the danger is that the end gas prepares itself before the flame arrives, so anything that shortens chemical delay (heat, pressure, reactive fuel) is bad. In the CI engine the danger is that fuel arrives and waits, so anything that shortens chemical delay is good. The same physics, the ignition delay of a hot mixture, has opposite roles.

answer: Fuels. Iso-octane resists autoignition (octane 100, very low cetane number); n-cetane ignites easily. A good petrol is a poor diesel fuel and the reverse; that is why the two ratings run in opposite directions.

Noise and damage. SI knock rings at about 6 to 7 kHz and attacks the piston crown and ring lands through local pressure and heat; diesel knock is a harder, lower-pitched clatter that loads the bearings and the whole structure. Both raise heat transfer to the walls.
Detection. Both are judged by the rate of pressure rise and by ringing, not by peak pressure: the diesel fuel B above has a slightly higher peak yet runs more quietly.

Judgement. SI knock is a hard limit that caps compression ratio and boost, managed today with knock sensors and fuel quality. Diesel knock is a noise and durability problem managed with injection control: pilot shots and rate shaping in common-rail systems have largely removed it in normal running, leaving cold starts as the main case.

bank.q: Evaluate the competing objectives in the design of an SI combustion chamber, using surface-to-volume ratio, flame path, squish and breathing. Recommend a chamber for a low-cost small car engine and justify it.
outline: Objectives and their conflicts
S/V numbers for disc and dome
Hemispherical, pent-roof, wedge, bathtub compared
Knock: time and density factors
Recommendation with cost
Judgement
answer: Objectives. High volumetric efficiency (large valves), short flame path (central plug, compact shape), high anti-knock quality (small, cool end gas), low surface-to-volume ratio (low heat loss, less quench), controlled turbulence, no hot spots, and low cost.

answer.text: Surface-to-volume ratio, with numbers. For Vc = 62.44 cm³ and bore 86 mm:

answer: The dome has 11 % less surface, so less heat loss and less quench area for unburnt hydrocarbons.

Conflicts. (1) Low S/V and big valves favour a dome, but a dome gives little squish, so the burn is slower at part load and turbulence must come from tumble ports. (2) Squish keeps the end gas cool and adds turbulence, but the squish band adds surface and crevices. (3) A high compression ratio raises efficiency but needs a compact, knock-resistant chamber and good cooling of the exhaust side. (4) Four valves and a central plug give the best burn and breathing but cost more in machining and valve gear.

answer.text: Shapes compared.

answer: Bore, compression ratio and cooling. A small bore shortens the flame path, so a cheaper chamber can still burn fast enough to avoid knock. The exhaust valve and plug are the hottest parts: the chamber should put the end gas on the cool inlet side, under a squish band, never against the exhaust valve. Good coolant flow round the exhaust seat and plug boss is part of the chamber design, not an extra.

Recommendation. For a low-cost small car engine (small bore, say 70 to 75 mm), a two-valve wedge or bathtub head with a good squish band and the plug as central as the valves allow. The small bore keeps the flame path short anyway (time factor), squish supplies turbulence and a cool end gas, and the single camshaft keeps cost down. It will run a compression ratio of about 10 on regular fuel.

If the budget allows: a four-valve pent-roof head with a central plug and tumble ports is better on every technical count (efficiency, power, emissions, knock margin), and is now common even in small cars because the extra cost is offset by fuel economy rules.

Judgement. Relax breathing first (two valves), not knock resistance: a chamber that knocks forces spark retard and loses more efficiency than the valves cost. Keep the flame path short, the end gas in a squish band, and the exhaust valve and plug well cooled.

bank.q: Analyse how turbulence from air motion affects flame speed, the rate of pressure rise, cycle-to-cycle variation and knock in an SI engine. What limits the amount of turbulence a designer should aim for?
outline: S<sub>T</sub> ≈ S<sub>L</sub> + u′
Burn duration and the p–θ trace, with numbers
Cyclic variation and the flame kernel
Knock: time factor
Limits: heat loss, pumping, flame quench, rough running
answer: Flame speed. In still gas petrol–air burns at SL ≈ 0.3 to 0.5 m/s. Turbulence wrinkles the front, so ST ≈ SL + u′, with u′ about half the mean piston speed. Since u′ rises with engine speed, the burn keeps about the same crank degrees at all speeds, which is what lets petrol engines run fast. For the worked examples' petrol engine at 3000 rev/min, the mean piston speed is 2 × 0.086 × 3000/60 = 8.6 m/s, so u′ ≈ 4.3 m/s and ST ≈ 0.4 + 4.3 ≈ 4.7 m/s, about eleven times the laminar value.

answer.text: Rate of pressure rise. A shorter burn raises dp/dθ and moves the peak towards TDC. In the worked examples' petrol engine (burn starting 10° bTDC):

answer: More turbulence moves the engine from the slow row towards the fast row: more work, cooler exhaust, but rougher running past about 3 bar/°CA.

Cycle-to-cycle variation. The early kernel is small, so the turbulence and mixture at the plug when the spark fires decide each cycle's burn. Well-organised motion (tumble breaking down at TDC) gives strong, repeatable turbulence and a fast early flame, so COVimep falls; in the ten-cycle example it is 1.3 %, against 13.7 % for a lean, slow-burning set.

Knock. Turbulence is a time factor: a faster flame reaches the end gas before its ignition delay runs out. Squish also keeps the end gas thin and close to the cool head. So more turbulence allows a higher compression ratio or more spark advance.

Limits. (1) Heat transfer: faster gas scrubs the walls, so heat loss rises with turbulence and can cancel the gain. (2) Volumetric efficiency: ports and masks that make swirl or tumble restrict the flow at full load. (3) Flame quench: very intense turbulence at the kernel can stretch and blow out a weak flame, worst with lean mixtures. (4) Rough running and NOx from very fast burns.

Where the turbulence comes from. Tumble from steep inlet ports in pent-roof heads is preferred in petrol engines, because the vortex breaks up just before the spark; squish adds turbulence at TDC and cools the end gas; swirl helps less in SI engines and costs flow area.

Conclusion. The aim is enough turbulence for a burn of about 25° to 35° (10 to 90 % burned about 20°), stable kernels and a good knock margin, delivered near TDC by tumble and squish rather than by losses in the intake.

glossary.def: The last SI stage, after peak pressure, when the remaining charge burns during expansion.
Ignition of a fuel–air mixture by its own temperature, with no spark or flame.
A measure of how easily a diesel fuel ignites; higher means a shorter delay.
The cylinder volume at TDC, including any bowl or pre-chamber.
Standard deviation divided by the mean, as a percentage.
In a CI engine, the time or crank angle from the start of injection to the start of combustion.
Severe, shock-driven knock; in many books simply another word for knock.
The temperatures at which given fractions of a fuel sample boil off.
The last part of the charge to burn, compressed and heated ahead of the flame.
Actual fuel–air ratio divided by the stoichiometric one; above 1 is rich.
The thin reaction zone between burnt gas and fresh charge.
Speed at which the flame front crosses the chamber, relative to the cylinder head.
Energy released by combustion per degree of crank angle, dQ/dθ.
Indicated mean effective pressure: indicated work per cycle divided by the swept volume.
The first SI stage, from the spark to the first pressure rise above motoring.
Autoignition of the end gas ahead of the flame, giving pressure oscillations and noise.
Cylinder pressure against crank angle with no combustion.
Percentage of iso-octane in a blend with n-heptane that knocks like the fuel.
A small chamber in the head of an IDI diesel, joined to the main chamber by a throat.
Ignition of the charge by a hot surface before the spark.
Vapour pressure of a fuel measured at 37.8 °C; a measure of front-end volatility.
The flat area where the piston crown comes close to the head at TDC.
Swirl speed of the charge divided by engine speed.
Rotation of the charge about an axis at right angles to the cylinder axis.
The r.m.s. fluctuation of gas velocity, u′.
